definition.text: A movement calling for public policy that tackles climate change while also creating jobs, supporting economic growth and reducing inequality.

facts.text: It draws on the idea that the climate crisis needs a large initiative like Roosevelt's New Deal.
On 22 October 2008 UNEP launched a Global Green New Deal in response to the Great Recession, aiming to create green jobs, boost the world economy and curb climate change.
In the UK, the Green New Deal Group and New Economics Foundation proposed one as a way out of the Great Recession.
The 2019 US resolution by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ed Markey called for moving to 100% renewable, zero-emission energy within 10 years.
Environmental justice is an explicit part of it, focusing on communities of color, Indigenous peoples and low-income communities.
The European Commission's 2019 European Green Deal is less ambitious on timing, aiming for carbon neutrality in 2050.
Many supporters of its goals doubt the feasibility of parts of it; one former US science adviser called the 2030 goal too optimistic.

title: Growth imperative

definition.text: The idea that an economy may be forced to grow, because firms, households or governments face serious harm without growth.

facts.text: At the micro level, it means firms or households must raise revenue or consumption to protect their income.
At the macro level, a political growth imperative exists if growth is needed to avoid economic and social instability, pushing goals such as climate mitigation below growth.
Marxist theory holds that competition forces firms to 'grow or die'; critics reply that a firm can stay profitable without growth by paying profits out as dividends.
Unemployment from technical progress without growth (Okun's law) is a central argument for the political imperative.
Proposed ways out include resource taxes, shorter working time, and fairer income distribution such as basic income.
Whether it is a meaningful concept at all, and which mechanism causes it, is disputed, including within the post-growth movement.

contested_note: Economists dispute whether any real growth imperative exists and what would cause it.

title: Monetary growth imperative
article: Growth imperative#Monetary system and the role of positive interest rates

definition.text: The claim that money created as interest-bearing debt forces the economy to keep growing.

facts.text: Hans Christoph Binswanger estimated a minimum necessary growth rate of 1.8%, Mathias Binswanger one of 0.45%.
Critics using stock-flow consistent models show repaid interest flows back into the economy, so debt can be serviced without growth if money is not hoarded.
On this view, the savings rate rather than the interest rate decides whether a non-growing economy is stable.

contested_note: Some authors find a growth imperative in interest-bearing money, while model-based critics say none arises from debt-based money as such.
